disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized mainly by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, restlessness, impulsive decision-making, and difficulty inhibiting responses, with inattention often present but less prominent. It typically begins in childhood and persists into adolescence and adulthood, with functional impairment in academic, occupational, or social domains required for diagnosis. Clinically, patients may come to attention when environmental demands for sustained effort, planning, or behavioral restraint increase, such as during higher education or more complex jobs. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, or disruptive behavior disorders by its early onset, cross-situational pervasiveness, and the pattern of chronic hyperactive/impulsive traits rather than episodic changes in behavior.

narrative.stressor: Cathleen’s hyperactive, project-driven style was praised in high school art and shop classes, where quick starts and constant movement were assets and teachers quietly accommodated her tendency to lose track of directions. The problems became more obvious about two years ago when she started taking community college business courses while trying to launch her handcrafted accessories shop online; she signed up for extra classes, overcommitted to collaborations, and found that the more structured coursework and deadlines clashed with her tendency to jump into new ideas mid-lecture and during study sessions. As assignments grew more complex and her e‑commerce work required longer stretches of focused, stepwise tasks, instructors and classmates began commenting on how she seemed to "check out" midway through instructions and then scramble to catch up, leading to dropped classes and stalled business plans. After failing a key accounting course, losing money on half-finished inventory, and hearing a professor suggest an evaluation for attention issues, she agreed to see a psychiatrist when her academic advisor linked her academic struggles and chaotic work habits to a possible underlying attention disorder.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I start out really motivated, but I keep zoning out when people explain what to do and end up not finishing my class assignments or business tasks the way they were asked.”

narrative.stressor: For most of his life, Edgar’s constant motion and spur-of-the-moment decisions were absorbed by informal jobs, family events, and church activities where structure was loose and others quietly redirected him. Over the past two years, escalating financial pressure on his household pushed him to take on more responsibility managing his family’s tight budget, coordinating his church’s food pantry logistics, and trying to secure a steady position as a community-center aide. The increased need to sit through planning meetings, handle detailed forms, and wait in lines for assistance programs clashed with his tendency to act before thinking, leading to missed benefits, errors in paperwork, and impulsive small purchases that undermined his carefully tracked spreadsheets, all of which heightened his anxiety about providing for his family. After a near eviction scare triggered by a series of impulsive financial decisions and missed appointments, his wife and parish priest both urged him to seek professional help, and he agreed when he realized his difficulty holding back and staying on track was directly jeopardizing their already fragile finances.
narrative.chief_complaint: “When there’s a line or a process, I just can’t seem to wait my turn without jumping ahead or changing plans, and it keeps messing up our money and appointments.”

narrative.stressor: Cathy had long relied on her intelligence and love of fast-paced problem-solving to succeed in software development, and her tendency to pace, gesture, and multitask during coding sessions was tolerated in startup environments. About two years ago, after being promoted to a senior role leading agile teams in a larger company, her days shifted from mostly hands-on coding to long planning meetings, code reviews, and mentoring sessions that demanded patient, sustained engagement and careful listening. In this more structured context, her long-standing restlessness and urge to move became harder to hide: colleagues noticed her frequently leaving her chair during sprints, drifting over to other desks mid-meeting, and appearing disengaged in video calls, which began to be reflected in performance feedback about her leadership presence. When a trusted manager framed the issue as a possible attention-regulation problem rather than a motivation issue and suggested an evaluation—echoing Cathy’s own worries about how hard it felt to simply stay put in meetings—she sought psychiatric consultation to understand and address what was interfering with her effectiveness at work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “In longer work meetings I just can’t stay in my seat—I keep getting up to move around even when I know it looks unprofessional.”
